📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham failed to overcome bottom side Preston North End in what was a desperately disappointing spectacle for West Ham fans who had been expecting so much more from their fresh manager’s first home game.

It has been revealed that A scrappy first goal conceded came from pretty much Preston’s only attempt at goal, and then our visitors sat back in time-honoured tradition. Four times the Hammers crashed the ball against the woodwork in a first half which revealed plenty of promise, however the second half evaporated in familiar fashion, inexplicably, no sooner than Mavropanos crashed in the equaliser.

Just about every fan expected West Ham to go on and win the game convincingly – yet instead they huffed and puffed with endless ‘after you – no after you’ short, sideways passes as nobody took responsibility for making the killer pass or – heaven forbid- taking on the shot.

However, the West Ham manager will no doubt do his best, tomorrow maybe, to pull out positives, despite being ‘devastated‘ at the result:.

Edson Álvarez, in his first game this season, El Machin was, surprisingly, up to speed pretty much immediately, sitting in front of the defence. He was everywhere: collecting, tidying up, harrying, attacking and breaking down opponents’ attacks. The late-tackling liability of last season was nowhere to be seen as he impressed and looks as if he has found himself a role for the coming weeks.

However, there’s a caveat: Remember this is the bottom side in the division who have just held us to draw. It will be intriguing to see if he copes against tougher opponents.

Edson Alvarez -Looked in control this afternoon – of his own discipline and of his midfield patch.

Finn Herrick: It can only have been unsettling, as the young keeper came to punch his first corner only to find a team mate’s glancing header got there first, looping the ball over his outstretched fists and allowing Preston to open the scoring against the run of play.

It has been revealed that credit to him, Herrick kept his cool and grew in stature as the game went on. He made an excellent double save after Mayers’ poor defensive header, and played well with the ball at his feet, combining Areola’s shot-stopping ability and Hermansen’s football skills.

However, positives aside, Parker has his work cut out simply to get this team’s work rate up. This time, they started quick and could have had three in the first half, even though there was a hesitancy and a lack of creation in front of goal.

Why it evaporated no sooner than the Hammers had equalised was a mystery. What should have become a barrage launched on Preston’s goal became a last thirty minutes of frustrating misfiring.

Just. Not. Good.Enough. Despite the bright points which Parker referenced in his post – match conference.

Just don’t blame West Ham’s newest manager for the failure of the last three to demand pacy, attacking football and recruiting so-called strikers who wouldn’t have made it into West Ham’s championships side of 2004/5 or 2011/12.

Recent findings suggest that can’t make a silk purse out of a sows ear. Especially not in two weeks.

Latest Update: West Ham 1-1 Preston: Scott Parker Still Struggling To Unlock Jarrod Bowen

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division.
  • Recent findings suggest that edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did.
  • The statistics certainly make for interesting reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham were nowhere near good enough against the worst team in the division. Whilst we had our chances, it would be a long stretch to suggest we were significantly better than Preston, particularly during a first half in which the visitors created opportunities of their own.

Recent findings suggest that edson Álvarez looked decent enough on his return to the team, but Scott Parker looks no closer to getting the best out of Jarrod Bowen than Nuno Espírito Santo or Graham Potter did. In essence, the Hammers lacked magic, and watching our best player pinned to the right flank was depressing.

The statistics certainly make for interesting reading. West Ham registered 30 attempts on goal, but only four were on target. We also hit the woodwork three times, with Bowen and Joël Veltman striking opposite posts during the same passage of play before Edvin Austbø rattled the crossbar shortly after half-time.

Preston took the lead through Liam Lindsay after just 18 minutes, following a corner which Joël Piroe inadvertently flicked towards his own goal.

Konstantinos Mavropanos eventually equalised on the hour mark, heading home Arne Engels’ cross after Manor Solomon had helped create the opening.

Yet even after drawing level, West Ham couldn’t find a winner against a team who arrived at the London Stadium bottom of the Championship.

In a recent development, there were chances, certainly. Tomáš Souček had a late header tipped over, while Mavropanos headed over in stoppage time. But for all the possession and pressure, there was precious little composure in front of goal.

And as far as I’m concerned, this was a match West Ham simply had to win.

What makes the situation particularly frustrating is that we’ve already seen what Bowen can do when he’s given more freedom.

Recent findings suggest that during the remarkable comeback against Cardiff City, our captain was allowed to drift into central positions, where he caused all sorts of problems. His movement, passing and ability to find space helped transform a game which had looked completely lost at half-time.

I was so impressed that I subsequently wrote about how Scott Parker needed to restore West Ham’s most dangerous weapon.

Unfortunately, against Blackburn, Bowen was back operating as a conventional right winger. And against Preston, we saw much the same thing.

It has been revealed that that’s not to suggest Bowen didn’t contribute. He was involved throughout and managed eight attempts on goal, including the effort which struck the post.

But there’s a difference between getting Bowen involved in the game and getting the best out of him.

West Ham have spent far too long relying on our captain to produce something special from wide positions, often with defenders able to anticipate where he’s going to receive the ball.

Against Cardiff, we briefly saw something different.

Bowen was the inspiration behind that second-half recovery. He looked far more dangerous when he was able to move into the middle and influence the game rather than remaining tied to the touchline.

I genuinely thought Parker had stumbled upon something which could change West Ham’s season.

Instead, two matches later, we seem to have gone backwards.

Of course, the manager has plenty of other issues demanding his attention.

In a recent development, there were some positives against Preston. Álvarez made his first Championship appearance for West Ham since May 2025 and looked reasonably comfortable in midfield, while young goalkeeper Finlay Herrick produced an excellent double save to prevent the visitors doubling their lead.

Mavropanos also deserves credit for another crucial goal, particularly given that he is a centre-back who continues to contribute at the other end of the pitch.

But the bigger picture remains deeply concerning.

West Ham simply had to start turning the London Stadium into somewhere opposition teams feared visiting.

Instead, the bottom club have come away with a point, and Parker has now overseen two draws and a defeat in his first three matches.

I appreciate he hasn’t been in the job long, and I’m not suggesting he’s solely responsible for problems which have been developing for some considerable time.

However, the international break gave him an opportunity to work with the players, and I had hoped to see considerably more improvement than we witnessed.

For me, the biggest concern remains our inability to get the best out of Bowen.

According to recent reports, we have a player capable of providing the creativity, movement and unpredictability that this team so desperately needs. Yet we’re still asking him to spend most of his time playing in the same predictable areas of the pitch.

West Ham don’t lack effort. Against Preston, they certainly didn’t lack possession or attempts on goal.

And until Scott Parker finds a way of giving Jarrod Bowen the freedom to provide it, I fear we’re going to see plenty more afternoons like this one.

Breaking: Mykhailo Mudryk reveals he spent 'MILLIONS' on legal bills to fight doping charge as he blames his stint with Ukraine for two-year ban in tell-all interview

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 19:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 02:46 EST, 19 November 2026.
  • Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed his stint with the Ukrainian national team for the failed doping test which cost him two years of his career and revealed how fighting his case personally cost him millions of pounds.
  • The Chelsea winger, who is now on loan with Tottenham Hotspur, has opened up for the first time since he returned to football in the summer when his suspension was suddenly lifted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Published: 19:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 02:46 EST, 19 November 2026.

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed his stint with the Ukrainian national team for the failed doping test which cost him two years of his career and revealed how fighting his case personally cost him millions of pounds.

The Chelsea winger, who is now on loan with Tottenham Hotspur, has opened up for the first time since he returned to football in the summer when his suspension was suddenly lifted.

It was in a two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel. While the title of the video mentions ‘suicidal thoughts’, Mudryk clarifies during the conversation that he did not consider committing suicide despite being in a dark place. ‘Kill myself – no, that’s not a way out,’ he stated when asked that question.

But he did discuss how Chelsea broke the news of his failed test to him, whether they helped their £89million signing from Shakhtar Donetsk during his ban, his belief that the drug meldonium entered his system while he was in Ukraine, and why he is now with Tottenham. He further claimed that he has faced threats from gangsters, and admitted his dream is to someday win the Ballon d’Or.

On the Ukrainian national team and their federation, the Ukrainian Association of Football, Mudryk stated: ‘I’ll be honest, it pretended to help. But in reality, there was no help. They created more problems than they solved. Especially when we needed help the most, they turned their backs on us.

'I just would like, for the future, everyone to understand that you can only rely on yourself.'.

Mykhailo Mudryk has spoken publicly for the first time about the doping case that cost him two years of his career.

Mudryk has criticised the Ukrainian Association of Football over their support during his case.

Daily Mail Sport contacted the Ukrainian Association of Football for comment.

Industry observers note that continuing, Mudryk stated: ‘The UAF is afraid of being left to blame in this situation, and afraid of the criticism or whatever else might come raining down. Distancing themselves from their own player, not helping, pretending to help, and in the end, first they drag the case out for months without really helping the case in the end. But at least the UAF isn’t to blame.’.

Mudryk was handed an initial four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test, with his last appearance prior to that coming in November 2024 in the Conference League away at Heidenheim. He scored in that 2-0 win for Chelsea. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'. Mudryk appeared for Chelsea during their pre-season tour before joining Tottenham on loan.

Sources indicate that on how and why he failed his test, Mudryk said: ‘I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It’s a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe.

Sources indicate that ‘This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that’s Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

‘I was at home and Chelsea’s management came to see me and they stated we needed to talk. Then they say you’ve returned a positive doping test and now you’re facing a ban.

‘You can’t believe it’s true. You can’t believe this is happening to you. If I’d ever taken anything anywhere, I’d have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

‘At least I’d have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that’s the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

It has been revealed that ‘Otherwise there’d be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don’t hear them.

Mudryk returned to action when his ban was lifted in August, with the winger revealing Xabi Alonso told him to get game time and that he was 'counting on him'.

The Ukrainian joined Tottenham on loan but has seen injury restrict his involvement to date.

Industry observers note that ‘At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you’re falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You’re flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don’t wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.’.

According to recent reports, mudryk revealed how ‘the figure is in the millions’ when asked about the lawyers fees which were needed to fight his case. He confirmed he paid for that himself, along with the personal trainers and massage therapists he used to maintain his fitness while suspended. However, Mudryk did add that Chelsea continued to pay his salary during his time out of football.

On joining Tottenham and being reunited with Roberto De Zerbi, who formerly managed him at Shakhtar Donetsk, Mudryk said: ‘It’s a perfectly logical decision. The club (Chelsea) has a newly introduced coach (Xabi Alonso), he sees football his own way. He sees the players he needs for that football. He came up and told me straight to my face: “You’d better go and play, get some game time, and then come back to Chelsea. I’m counting on you.”’ On De Zerbi, he added: ‘We met and he claims: “Are you happy? Come on, we’ve still got a lot of work to do together.”’.

Sources indicate that mudryk added how difficult it was after switching to England and, along with encountering problems with his former representatives who encouraged him to move to Chelsea rather than Arsenal, he said: 'They give you ultimatums, you know. That’s how it is.’.

Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing

📅 17 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.
  • This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.
  • But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

This particular evening belonged to Floyd, though. Deployed as a lone striker by Enzo Maresca, you would not have known he ordinarily plays as a midfielder such was the confidence and composure the 17-year-old oozed.

Norwich could not live with him or City for that matter as Maresca’s impressive start as manager since replacing Pep Guardiola continued apace.

This must have been an incredibly satisfying moment for Samba Sr. He came through incredible hardship – at one stage as a teenager he was rough-sleeping – to forge an impressive career totalling more than 450 games for club and country.

So to be in a position to now have three sons in City’s academy and one produce a debut like this will fill him with enormous pride. Floyd was later seen enjoying a warm embrace with his dad in the crowd, moments after being congratulated by Tyrone, a year his senior, and 12-year-old Emerson, who plays for City’s Under-13s.

“I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team – to get a debut like that is mind blowing,” Samba mentioned. “I couldn’t believe it myself, but that’s just the beginning, I’ve got a major career ahead of me. It was a great debut.”.

Industry observers note that floyd caught the eye with a fine free-kick in City’s 2-1 FA Youth Cup final victory over Manchester United last season and now he has goals for the senior side to his name. Pretty stunning they were, too.

The first was a superbly steered header past two Norwich bodies on the line from Allan’s cross and the second a lovely, nonchalantly curled finish low into the far corner.

It has been revealed that what a moment for Floyd Samba! 😍A goal on his Man City debut for the 17-year-old, son of former Blackburn defender Chris 🩵 pic.twitter.com/VCVfX9HCNn.

Chris Samba has deliberately kept a low profile, keen to let his sons get on with their own careers free of distractions, but there was no chance he was going to be able to suppress his emotions in that instant. And nor should he. It was some moment for the boy and his family.

As impressed as Maresca was by the goals, it will have been other elements of Samba’s game that also caught the eye. He did extremely well to hold off the attentions of Norwich’s centre-backs when receiving a pass from Ayyoub Bouaddi and then returning the ball to the Moroccan who released Rayan Cherki through to score City’s second. His movement was also sharp, at one point taking a difficult pass sweetly in an adjusted strike, only for Norwich’s Bruno Alves to come across to make a timely intervention before Samba could get his shot off.

"Was there any doubt?"Ayyoub Bouaddi with his first assist for Man City as he sets up Rayan Cherki to make it 2-0 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0gfxp5GDXy.

“It was satisfying not just for the two goals but for the entire performance,” Maresca said. “He didn’t play many games as a nine but he was good. He’s young, full of energy, strong, he can finish.”.

Recent findings suggest that allan, a £34m summer signing from Palmeiras, will have been just as pleased with his contribution. Maresca’s fluid formation initially resembled a 3-1-5-1 with Allan effectively operating as a right wing-back but he stuck doggedly to the task before eventually getting the moment to showcase his quality, first with his cross for Samba and later with a neat solo run and finish.

Driving inside Sam Field and then cutting back inside the Norwich man before curling an inch perfect finish into the bottom corner – all of it done with his left foot – it was quite the introduction.

Industry observers note that allan on his debut! 🇧🇷Magic from the Brazilian to make it 3-0 to Man City 💥 pic.twitter.com/nw6lNqh1yL.

Hugo Viana, City’s director of football, has said supporters will need to be patient with Allan and that it may take the 22-year-old time to adjust to English football but this first outing will do his confidence plenty of good.

“It was important for him to play 90 minutes and to see a little bit the English competition that is a bit different from South America so overall was good,” Maresca mentioned.

It has been revealed that cherki was the only survivor from the team that started Sunday’s victory over Manchester United but it all felt pretty seamless from City. Bouaddi, the £85m signing from Lille, was poised and graceful in midfield alongside the impressive Mateo Kovacic and Geronimo Rulli could not have asked for a much quieter debut in goal.

FLOYD SAMBA again!! 🌟The 17-year-old curls one in to score his second on his Man City debut with his dad Christopher watching on in the stands 👏 pic.twitter.com/fJ5mfEWBx1.

In a recent development, nico O’Reilly looked like he had barely broken a sweat despite Norwich’s players routinely being unable to keep up with him. Norwich themselves made nine changes but the gulf in class was enormous and testament to City’s strength in depth.

The game also gave Maresca the opportunity to give run outs to two more academy graduates who played in that Youth Cup final triumph, Kaden Braithwaite and Ryan McAidoo and the latter got his own name on the scoresheet to make it 5-0.

According to recent reports, all told there were seven City academy graduates on the pitch, two of them playing for Norwich. This was certainly a night to remember for the club’s youth production line.

With the dominant performance, Man City have earned themselves the privilege of hosting Brighton in the next round, who will no doubt prove a much stiffer challenge than Norwich. They become the sixth all-Premier League tie in the next round, with only Fleetwood, Bradford and Peterborough remaining from outside the top flight:.

Possession: Man City 66% vs 34% Norwich.

Touches inside opposition box: 30 vs 4.

It has been revealed that erling Haaland left out of the squad, watching from the stands, would have enjoyed that performance from Floyd Samba. Here is his second goal for you to enjoy on his debut night:.

FLOYD SAMBA again!! 🌟The 17-year-old curls one in to score his second on his Man City debut with his dad Christopher watching on in the stands 👏 pic.twitter.com/fJ5mfEWBx1.

Five unanswered goals and a home-grown hero emerges for Manchester City!

Industry observers note that great through ball from O’Reilly, which Lewis lets run past him for the dummy. McAidoo runs on to it on the right of the box and first-time fires it low into the far corner.

It has been a perfect night for Manchester City’s academy.

Well we look like we’re heading for a matching scoreline to the previous edition of the fixture. That pesky shot on target is still eluding Norwich, whereas Samba is still out there looking for his hat-trick.

Two minutes of time to be added – who will get there first?

O’Reilly sends a high, looping ball to the back post from the left side, where McAidoo rushes to meet it but can’t get over it under pressure.

Final change for Norwich, as Kvistgaarden who has not had much service tonight, comes off for Schwartau.

Bouaddi sends a looping ball across the field to McAidoo, which he picks up on the edge of the box, but he is unable to get the ball under control to take his shot and it is cleared away as far as another City shirt.

The corner comes in to the centre of the box but is headed out by a City shirt.

It’s all slightly too little too late for Norwich.

They get another corner as Musaba tries to send a cross into the box from the right and it is blocked out.

Industry observers note that A free-kick for Norwich now as O’Reilly commits the foul 35 yards out. It goes in towards McConville at the back post, but Ait-Nouri heads it out for a Norwich corner.

In a recent development, mo Touré strays just offside on the edge of the box, as Musaba sends a lovely little ball over to find him on the turn and the forward slots it past Rulli. Celebrations don’t quite begin before the flag goes up but that is a shame for the visitors.

Norwich have managed to get more of a grip in this half, despite conceding two more goals, but they are still without a shot on goal as we approach the final 15 minutes.

Another round of changes for both sides.

Man City take off scorer of their third goal Allan to bring on Braithwaite.

Norwich replace Ben Slimane and Bruno Alves with Touré and McConville.

Samba again at the heart of the action, laying off the ball to McAidoo on the right for the winger to run into the box. His shot towards the far post is saved low by Grimshaw who spills it almost into the path of Lewis, but Norwich survive.

Industry observers note that lewis makes a run down the right-hand side and crosses into Samba on the edge of the box. He lays off to McAidoo, but his shot goes sailing over the bar.

A surprise to no one, it is chucking it down in Manchester.

Big cheers from the away end as Norwich get their first corner of the evening. It is lofted high and long to the back post, where it is headed away by Bouaddi. It bounces out to Musaba, who has just come on, and he strikes it from the top of the box on the half-volley.

His shot cuts through a crowd in the box and has Rulli diving to his left, but it goes wide of the post. What an introduction that would have been!

According to recent reports, well all the stories from this match will be all about young Floyd Samba. Feel free to leave your best punny Samba/dance-related headlines in the comments section.

For Man City as you would expect it is all about game management from here on out.

Some more changes to report for Norwich as well, as Crnac is replaced by Musaba.

Wright is able to run in to space towards the edge of the box, but as has been their story all evening, his pass out to the wing is just not where it needs to be and their effort just breaks down.

What a way to score a second! A night to remember for Floyd Samba!

Norwich try and play out from the back but far too sloppy and Ait-Nouri picks up the ball on the left of the box. He has plenty of time to tee up Samba inside the box at the left corner, who finds himself with plenty of space to curl his shot into the far corner, beating the diving Grimshaw.

We may be seeing plenty more of him this season.

In a recent development, norwich looking for their way back into the game, as the ball comes down the left, fizzed in low and flashes past Rulli, trying to claim it. It deflects off a crowd of bodies and spins up, but Fisher can’t connect and it spins away harmlessly wide of the goal.

It is definitely Norwich’s best chance of the game and Fisher will be upset he hasn’t made more of that.

And Allan makes it three! Minutes after the restart, the Brazilian makes his own mark on his debut.

Maresca switched him onto the left side to escape Yongwa, and he picks up the ball outside the box and makes the run inside. He runs circles around Field and slots the ball home into the far bottom corner.

Sources indicate that some changes from both sides at half-time. McAidoo comes on for Cherki, though O’Reilly is the one to move up into midfield to fill the gap.

Norwich take off Diallo for Maghoma.

45 minutes left for the visitors to create something special!

It has been revealed that what a moment for Floyd Samba! 😍A goal on his Man City debut for the 17-year-old, son of former Blackburn defender Chris 🩵 pic.twitter.com/VCVfX9HCNn.

Manchester City will be the ones to host Brighton in the next round – giving the visitors the opportunity to pull off a remarkable feat of knocking out both Manchester sides should they win.

Enjoy the highlights from last night as they came from behind to dispatch Man Utd:.

A few minutes to remember here for Floyd Samba. First he steers home a very well taken header to give City the lead and then he plays a crucial role in the second, holding the ball up well before laying it off to Bouaddi to release Cherki to score. That’s how to make an impression on your debut.

And the floodgates have opened. Two goals in two minutes for the defending champions.

We broke down the incident as it happened on Sunday and you can get the full story here.

Heavy squad rotation (10 changes in total for Maresca) has handed debuts for Gero Rulli in goal, as well as Allan and Floyd Samba in the outfield.

17-year-old Samba is the latest from City’s academy to be making his debut in the senior squad, following in the footsteps of Phil Foden, Rico Lewis, Nico O’Reilly and many more. A versatile midfielder, he has totalled 24 appearances across six competitions (incl Premier League 2) and scored 17 and assisted six goals in those matches.

Keep your eyes on young midfielder Floyd Samba, who has been handed his Manchester City debut tonight against Norwich by manager Enzo Maresca. Floyd is the 17 year old son of former Blackburn Rovers defender Christopher Samba.

Sources indicate that his older brother Tyrone, 18, also plays for City. The siblings played in City’s FA Youth Cup final win over Manchester United last season, with Floyd scoring the first in a 2-1 win.

It has been revealed that city fans will also be keen to see how Allan Elias gets on on his first start, having arrived from Palmeiras for £34m. Geronimo Rulli also debuts in goal.

In a recent development, good evening and welcome to another night of Carabao Cup coverage! It is the final fixture of round three (I promise) as Manchester City host Norwich.

Industry observers note that these two sides have not met since 2022, when Norwich were still in the top flight and were beaten 4-0 by City. Looking at their previous meetings, the odds are definitely stacked in favour of Enzo Maresca’s side, who have scored 14 unanswered goals in their last three meetings with Norwich, while the Championship side have not scored any.

City will be looking to make it six straight wins across all competitions tonight, having started perfectly in the Premier League with four wins from four, and comfortably seeing off Porto in their Champions League opener.

They were the talk of the weekend with their deeply controversial 1-0 win over rivals Manchester United as – having gone down to 10 men after Phil Foden was sent off – their winning goal was allowed to stand despite Enzo Fernández being clearly in an offside position that impacted United’s keeper and backline.

City are defending their title in this competition – beating Arsenal last year in the final – but like all Premier League teams playing in European competitions, have only entered the tournament this year in the third round.

In a recent development, philippe Clement’s side beat MK Dons 4-1 in the first round, and followed that up with a 2-1 win over Cardiff City in the second to reach the Etihad tonight. The fourth-round draw has already been done, and it has been decided that the winner of this match will face Brighton.

But we have at least 90 minutes of the third round left before that, so without further ado, we’ll get underway and bring you team updates shortly!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 13:39.

Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face Hull City on Sunday as Fabian Hurzeler's side look to extend their impressive run of form in the clubs' first-ever Premier League meeting.

Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th after 10 matches and three points clear of the relegation zone, having gone eight league games without a victory despite remaining unbeaten on home soil this season.

Conversely, the Seagulls arrive full of confidence after recording consecutive top-flight wins over Manchester City and Brentford, boasting six clean sheets across their last seven league outings.

Here, Sports Mole takes a closer look at the head-to-head record and past meetings between Hull and Brighton.

Nearly 67 years have passed since Hull City and Brighton & Hove Albion first locked horns - a November 1959 Division Two clash that ended in a 3-1 victory for the Tigers - and there have now been 51 competitive meetings between the two clubs in all competitions.

The Seagulls hold the bragging rights when it comes to overall victories with 22, while Hull have claimed 15 wins of their own and another 14 contests have seen the spoils shared.

Remarkably, none of those 51 encounters have taken place in the Premier League, with every previous battle arriving in the Football League or the FA Cup, and the two sides have not crossed paths since a goalless Championship stalemate in East Yorkshire in February 2016.

Recent clashes between the pair have been notably tight, low-scoring affairs, with none of their last nine meetings across all competitions settled by more than a single goal and three ending 0-0.

During the 2015-16 campaign, both clubs collected a narrow 1-0 victory on home soil - Brighton prevailing in the Championship in September 2015 before Hull gained revenge in the FA Cup four months later - prior to that goalless draw in February.

Indeed, home advantage has heavily dictated this fixture in the modern era, as Hull are unbeaten in their last six home games against Brighton across all competitions - winning four and keeping five clean sheets - since suffering a 2-0 Division Three defeat in October 2000.

Conversely, the Tigers have endured a miserable record on the South Coast, failing to win any of their last 22 visits to Brighton since recording their sole away triumph in this fixture - a 2-1 Division Three success - way back in August 1965.

Brighton built much of their overall head-to-head lead during a dominant spell in the late 1980s and 1990s, rattling off four straight victories between October 1989 and April 1991 before later embarking on a nine-match unbeaten run from April 1993 to December 1996.

That sequence included the Seagulls' biggest-ever win in this matchup, a resounding 4-0 Division Two triumph in March 1996, while they also completed a comfortable league double over Hull with 2-0 and 3-0 victories in the 2000-01 Division Three season.

Hull's most emphatic triumph came in the highest-scoring meeting between the two sides, a 5-2 Division Two victory in December 1988, while they also put three unanswered goals past Brighton in March 1997.

The two teams have also collided five times in the FA Cup, with Brighton winning the first two ties in January 1985 (1-0) and January 1986 (3-2) before Hull turned the tide by edging a 2-1 replay victory in February 2014 following a 1-1 draw and claiming that 1-0 success in January 2016.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p-wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs.
  • Unconventional symmetry breaking in itinerant fermion systems has revealed some of the most remarkable phases of quantum matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of p-wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs. 1,2,3). Achieving p-wave superconductivity4 and its magnetic analogue5—characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric, p-wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge6,7. Despite recent progress in identifying candidate p-wave magnets5,7,8,9,10, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal p-wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves Sy polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted Sy exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics10, topological matter7, superconductivity11 and beyond.

Unconventional symmetry breaking in itinerant fermion systems has revealed some of the most remarkable phases of quantum matter. A celebrated example is p-wave superfluidity in helium-3, where odd-parity Cooper pairing generates emergent orders beyond conventional paradigms1,2,3. Its magnetic analogue, the p-wave magnet, is characterized by an odd-parity spin-polarized electronic structure that preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation while breaking inversion symmetry5,6.

Sources indicate that recently, spin group theory has provided a framework for identifying such magnetic states5, extending concepts developed for altermagnets12. Whereas ferromagnets exhibit conventional s-wave-like spin splitting and altermagnets exhibit even-parity d-, g- or i-wave spin order12,13, p-wave magnets are characterized by odd-parity spin polarization associated with commensurate coplanar magnetic order that breaks inversion symmetry while preserving a combined time-reversal and translation symmetry5,14. The resulting electronic structure can exhibit a single symmetry-allowed spin component, symmetry-enforced nodal planes and a characteristic momentum-dependent spin texture. Candidate p-wave magnetism has recently been explored in insulating NiI2 (ref. 8) and metallic Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12 (ref. 9). However, spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the characteristic odd-parity electronic spin texture remains limited8,9.

Here we present evidence for p-wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level (near-EF) electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi by combining symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations, neutron scattering and photoemission spectroscopy. Neutron diffraction reveals a commensurate spiral phase with propagation vector (0, 1/3, 0) below the upper magnetic transition temperature, TN1 ≈ 62 K, followed by a transition to a conical phase at the lower magnetic transition temperature, TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Magnetotransport measurements indicate strong coupling between magnetism and itinerant electrons. Below TN1, spin-integrated angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, associated with strong 4f–5d exchange coupling. Spin-ARPES provides spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for the expected odd-parity Sy polarization in the near-EF spectral features: the extracted polarization changes sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Because the near-EF spin-resolved features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, the observed Sy modulation is best interpreted as a spectroscopic signature of the expected p-wave spin texture at the level of the reconstructed electronic structure. Magnetic force microscopy (MFM) and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-µm chiral magnetic domains. Together, these observations identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating p-wave magnetism in electronic band structures and related spin-symmetry-based phenomena.

It has been revealed that in conventional ferromagnets and altermagnets (Fig. 1a), broken time-reversal symmetry permits even-parity spin-polarized electronic structures12. In the non-relativistic limit, conventional ferromagnets exhibit s-wave-like spin splitting, whereas altermagnets can exhibit d-, g- or i-wave-like spin-splitting patterns12,13,15,16,17,18. By contrast, unconventional odd-parity magnets can host p-, f- or h-wave spin polarization that preserves time-reversal (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\))-related symmetry while breaking inversion (\(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)) symmetry5. Commensurate chiral magnetic structures provide a natural route to such \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\)-symmetry breaking. In particular, coplanar non-collinear exchange fields can generate odd-parity spin polarization in momentum space when the magnetic structure preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) (ref. 5). As in conventional antiferromagnets, this symmetry enforces zero net magnetization in the ideal p-wave magnetic state (Fig. 1a).

Recent findings suggest that a, Schematic magnetic orders and their associated s-wave (ferromagnetic), d-wave (altermagnetic) and p-wave spin splitting in momentum space. Magenta and cyan spheres represent magnetic atoms with opposite spin orientations, related by the indicated combined spin–space symmetry operations in the d- and p-wave states, whereas blue spheres represent nonmagnetic atoms. b, Spiral magnetic structure of EuSi. The characteristic p-wave spin group symmetries are spin rotation combined with a glide mirror plane \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}{\bf{t}}]\), and with a lattice translation \([{C}_{2}{||}{\bf{t}}]\), respectively. c, Calculated spin-polarized Fermi surface of the spiral phase, including SOC, showing p-wave spin polarization and spin splitting. d, Calculated spin textures near the top of the valence bands in the kz = 0 (bottom) and kx = 0 (top) planes, with (left) and without (right) SOC. e, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersion along the −Ym–Г–Ym (ky) direction in the spiral phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC. f, Conical magnetic structure of EuSi, with the combined spin-rotation and translation symmetry \([{C}_{6}{||}{{\bf{t}}}^{{\prime} }]\) indicated. g, Calculated spin-polarized band dispersions along the same momentum direction in the conical phase, with (left) and without (right) SOC.

Sources indicate that we next consider the symmetry of the experimentally determined magnetic structures of EuSi. The crystal belongs to the point group D2h (space group Cmcm), and its magnetic states without (with) considering the effect of spin–orbit coupling (SOC) are described by the corresponding spin (magnetic) space group7. For the spiral state below TN1 ≈ 62 K, the spin space group is \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{y}}1\), which satisfies the criteria for collinear p-wave spin polarization in momentum space. The spin space group breaks the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{P}}\) symmetry, thereby allowing odd-parity spin polarization. The coplanarity of the magnetic moments, together with the spin-only symmetry \({C}_{2y}{\mathcal{T}}=[{M}_{y}|1]\,{=}^{{m}_{y}}1\), constrains the spin polarization to the y direction in momentum space. Combined with the \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) symmetry, the spin group symmetry prohibits the spin components Sx and Sz, while allowing a \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\)-symmetric Sy component satisfying:.

The spin-degenerate nodal plane at ky = 0, where ky is the component of the electron crystal momentum k = (kx, ky, kz) along the reciprocal-space direction corresponding to the crystallographic b axis, is protected by the combined spin rotation, lattice mirror and translation symmetry \([{C}_{2z}{||}{M}_{y}t]\), as illustrated in Fig. 1b. The corresponding spin-polarized electronic-structure calculations are shown in Fig. 1c–e. Figure 1d illustrates the calculated p-wave spin–momentum locking near the top of the valence band in the (kx, ky, 0) and (0, ky, kz) planes. The calculated bands obey the symmetry relations:.

It has been revealed that here, E(kx,ky,kz,Sy) denotes the electronic band energy at crystal momentum k for a state with spin polarization Sy along the b direction. Comparison of calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 1c–e) reveals that the characteristic p-wave spin polarization and splitting arise predominantly from the non-relativistic magnetic exchange, with only minor modifications from SOC. These calculations therefore provide the symmetry and electronic-structure framework for the p-wave state expected from the spin and magnetic (\({P}_{C}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}{2}_{1}\)) space groups of the experimentally determined spiral magnetic structure.

We next consider the conical state below TN2 ≈ 33.4 K. Its spin space group takes the ferromagnetic form \({{}^{{2}_{y}}C}^{1}{m}^{{m}_{x}}{c}^{1}{m}^{{6}_{y}}{t}^{{\prime} }\), characterized by a symmetry combining a six-fold spin rotation with translation, [\({C}_{6y}{|}{t}^{{\prime} }\)], as shown in Fig. 1f. Figure 1g shows the calculated electronic structure without and with SOC. The calculated dispersions of the spiral and conical phases are similar over much of momentum space but differ near the Γ point (Fig. 1e,g). In the conical phase, broken \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}\) lifts the spin degeneracy at the Γ point that is protected in the spiral phase (see Supplementary Note 1 for further symmetry analysis). Accordingly, an anomalous Hall response is symmetry-allowed in the conical phase but prohibited in the spiral phase. The magnetic space groups of both phases are chiral.

Sources indicate that euSi crystallizes in space group Cmcm (No. 63; Supplementary Tables 1–3). Single crystals were grown by the Bridgman method. Scanning transmission electron microscopy indicates high crystalline quality with few crystalline defects (Supplementary Fig. 2), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analysis yielded an Eu:Si ratio of 50.2:49.8, consistent with stoichiometric EuSi within instrumental uncertainty (Supplementary Fig. 3). Two magnetic transitions occur at TN1 ≈ 62 K and TN2 ≈ 33.4 K, together with a weak structural distortion near the structural distortion temperature TS ≈ 60 K (Supplementary Fig. 4). Magnetization measurements along the three crystallographic axes show no pronounced hysteresis (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating the absence of net magnetic moments at zero field. Upon cooling, these phase transitions define two boundaries: from the paramagnetic to the spiral magnetic phase, and subsequently to the conical magnetic phase (discussed later). Upon applying a magnetic field along the crystal’s a, b and c axes (Fig. 1f), the conical magnetic/spiral magnetic state exhibits metamagnetic transitions associated with spin-flop processes, and eventually evolves into a spin-polarized state at high fields (Supplementary Fig. 6c,f,i). Angular-dependent susceptibility further indicates a pronounced two-fold magnetic anisotropy (Supplementary Fig. 7).

The magnetic transitions at TN1 = 62 K and TN2 = 33.4 K, and structural distortion at TS = 59.7 K, are labelled. b, Magnetization versus magnetic field along the three crystallographic axes at 2 K and 40 K. The inset magnifies the low-field region, showing no distinct hysteresis. c, Resistivity of crystal S1 with current along a. The residual resistivity ratio, RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K), is approximately 262. d,e, Neutron-diffraction patterns in the (H, K, 1) plane at 40 K (d) and 6 K (e). f, Temperature evolution of the (0, 4, 0) and adjacent k1 satellite peaks between 5 K and 70 K. g,h, Refined spiral and conical magnetic structures at 40 K (g) and 6 K (h). The reference Eu moment in the a–c plane is aligned along a. This convention differs from Fig. 1 by a global rotation within the a–c plane, preserving the relative moment configuration and magnetic symmetry. i, Temperature-dependent intensities of representative k1 and k2 peaks, (0, 5/3, 1) and (0, 2, 1). The dashed lines mark the magnetic transitions. CM, conical magnetic; SM, spiral magnetic; PM, paramagnetic. f.u., formula unit; r.u.l., reciprocal lattice units; Q, scattering vector; j, electrical current density.

In a recent development, the longitudinal resistivity is metallic, with a residual resistivity ratio (RRR = ρxx(300 K)/ρxx(2 K) ≈ 262), where ρxx is the longitudinal electrical resistivity (Fig. 2c). A sharp resistivity change near TN1 and pronounced transport anisotropy accompany the magnetic transitions (Supplementary Fig. 8). Magnetotransport measurements further reveal a large, non-saturating magnetoresistance at low temperature (reaching 4,600% at 2 K with a 9 T magnetic field along b) (Supplementary Figs. 9–12). With increasing temperature towards the spiral magnetic state, the magnetoresistance becomes negative and remains so up to room temperature, indicating strong magnetic scattering in both the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic states.

To determine the magnetic structures, we performed single-crystal neutron diffraction (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Note 5). At 40 K, satellite peaks appear at (H, K, L) ± (0, 1/3, 0) (Fig. 2d), corresponding to a magnetic propagation vector k1 = (0, 1/3, 0). Magnetic-structure refinement identifies an spiral magnetic order with moments rotating in the a–c (010) plane (Fig. 2g). The spins are approximately ferromagnetically aligned within each double layer and rotate by π/3 between adjacent double layers, corresponding to a threefold magnetic periodicity along b. This commensurate coplanar spiral is consistent with the symmetry requirements for the p-wave magnetic state discussed above.

On cooling to 6 K, the k1 satellite peaks remain, while additional magnetic intensity develops at the structural Bragg positions, corresponding to a second magnetic propagation vector k2 = (0, 0, 0) (Fig. 2e). Refinement demonstrates that this component corresponds to a ferromagnetic moment along b, yielding the conical magnetic structure shown in Fig. 2h. The persistence of the k1 intensity across TN2 supports the coexistence of the spiral and b-axis components within the conical magnetic phase rather than macroscopic phase separation. The refined ordered moments are mac = 4.4(1) μB per Eu at 40 K and mac = 5.4(1) μB per Eu, mb = 4.1(1) μB per Eu at 6 K, where μB is the Bohr magneton, consistent with the Eu2+ valence inferred from X-ray absorption and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements (Supplementary Fig. 14).

The temperature dependence of representative magnetic peaks further resolves the two transitions (Fig. 2f,i). The k1 order develops below TN1, whereas the k2 component appears below TN2. Critical exponent fits yield β = 0.32(2) for k1 and β = 0.33(3) for k2, slightly below the classical three-dimensional Heisenberg value (β = 0.365), possibly reflecting additional spin–lattice coupling.

Before turning to the spin-resolved measurements relevant for p-wave magnetism, we first characterize the overall electronic structure of EuSi across the magnetic transitions (Fig. 3). The calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the spiral magnetic phase (Fig. 3b) contains several electron/hole pockets exhibiting strong anisotropy along the kx, ky and kz directions. Figure 3c shows the measured band structure in the kx–kz plane, corresponding to the cleaved a–c (010) plane in the conical magnetic phase. The constant-energy contours (Fig. 3c) show clear C2 symmetry and are broadly consistent with the calculated Fermi surface; similar dispersions are observed in the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases.

High-symmetry points are labelled. b, Calculated three-dimensional Fermi surface in the magnetic BZ in the spiral magnetic phase. c, Constant-energy contours at EF (i), EF − 0.1 eV (ii) and EF  − 0.2 eV (iii) in the kx–kz plane measured at 10 K. d,e, ARPES dispersion along the \(\overline{{\rm{Z}}}-\overline{\Gamma }-\overline{{\rm{X}}}\) direction, measured at 57 eV (ky ≈ 2π/b; d) and corresponding calculated bands (ky ≈ 2π/b; e). Here, b is the crystal lattice constant. f,g, ARPES dispersions measured with 7 eV photons (ky ≈ 2π/b; f) and corresponding DFT calculations at ky ≈ 2π/b (g) in the conical magnetic (i), spiral magnetic (ii) and paramagnetic (iii) phases. The α, β and γ bands are labelled. h, Temperature-dependent energy-distribution curves integrated near \(\overline{\Gamma }\) over the shaded region in f(i). Fitting resolves the peaks associated with α, β and γ. i, Temperature-dependent peak energies obtained from the energy-distribution curve fits. j, Corresponding energy separations between α and γ, β and γ, and α and β. Error bars in i represent energy uncertainties estimated from the energy resolution of the 7-eV laser-ARPES set-up at each temperature; those in j represent the corresponding propagated uncertainties in the energy separations.

The measured dispersion along the corresponding high-symmetry direction exhibits dispersive Eu 5d bands crossing EF (Fig. 3d). The measurement geometry, orbital-character analysis and determination of the high-symmetry points for the a–c cleavage plane are described in Supplementary Figs. 15 and 16. The bands near the \(\overline{\Gamma }\) point are labelled α, β and γ, and the band near the zone boundary is denoted φ, following comparison with the density functional theory (DFT) calculations in Fig. 3e. Differences in the number and precise positions of the calculated and measured bands may arise from the simplified treatment of magnetic structure, calculation parameters such as effective on-site Coulomb interaction U and lattice constant, and many-body effects (Supplementary Note 10).

Sources indicate that over a wider energy range, ARPES reveals the Eu 4f- and Si 3p-derived states (Supplementary Fig. 17). The Eu 4f flat bands, labelled FB1–FB3, lie approximately 1–2 eV below EF and are further identified by resonant ARPES measurements (Supplementary Fig. 18). These states are crossed by dispersive Si 3p bands, consistent with orbital-projected calculations. Their location well below EF is consistent with the localized 4f 7 configuration and large local Eu2+ moment.

The magnetic transitions are accompanied by a pronounced reconstruction of the near-EF electronic structure. High-resolution laser-ARPES demonstrates that the α, β and γ bands evolve strongly across the conical magnetic, spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases (Fig. 3f). Their characteristic energies shift by approximately 50 meV between the conical magnetic and spiral magnetic phases, followed by a more pronounced reconstruction at TN1, where the three bands merge upon entering the paramagnetic phase (Supplementary Fig. 19). Tracking their energy positions from energy-distribution curve fits (Fig. 3h–j) highlights that this reconstruction follows the temperature evolution of the in-plane magnetic order k1 determined by neutron diffraction (Fig. 2i). The calculations (Fig. 3g) reproduce the main evolution in the spiral magnetic and paramagnetic phases, whereas larger deviations occur in the conical magnetic phase, suggesting that the additional b-axis ferromagnetic component has a comparatively smaller influence on the near-EF electronic structure. Similar evolution of the α, β, γ and φ bands is observed at different photon energies and momentum directions (Supplementary Figs. 20 and 21), indicating a robust magnetism-driven reconstruction of the Eu 5d electronic structure.

In a recent development, we attribute this reconstruction to the strong 5d–4f exchange coupling between the localized Eu 4f moments and itinerant Eu 5d electrons through intra-atomic exchange19,20. This exchange lifts the spin degeneracy and accounts for the large band splitting with a gap of approximately 100 meV (ref. 21). Once the spiral magnetic/conical magnetic order develops, the enlarged magnetic unit cell also imposes a periodic exchange potential that folds the reconstructed 5d bands. This interpretation is consistent with the observed substantial Eu moment22. The Si p bands also show reconstruction across TN1, whereas the Eu 4f bands remain nearly unchanged in energy, although the intensity of FB1 starts to decrease at TN2 (Supplementary Fig. 22).

Sources indicate that the dominant effect of the a–c-plane magnetic moments is further reflected in the reconstructed electronic structure across multiple momentum planes, arising from the combined effects of exchange splitting and magnetic-zone folding. Consistent reconstruction is observed by ARPES on both the cleaved b–c (100) and a–b (001) surfaces (Supplementary Note 8).

In a recent development, we probe the predicted p-wave symmetry using spin-resolved ARPES on the a–c cleavage plane at 40 K. The relevant symmetry relations predict opposite Sy polarization under \({k}_{y}\to -{k}_{y}\), \(E(0,{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\,=\) \(E(0,-{k}_{y},{k}_{z},-{S}_{y})\) and unchanged Sy under the corresponding \({k}_{x}\to -{k}_{x}\), \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) operation. By varying the photon energy, we sample a series of ky values across successive magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4a,b; additional measurements from an independent facility are shown in Supplementary Fig. 34). At \(({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z})\,=\) \((0,0.3\times 2{\rm{\pi }}/b,0)\) (cut 1 in Fig. 4d; b is the magnetic-supercell lattice constant), the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions show negative, positive and negative Sy polarization of approximately 5%, respectively. At the corresponding negative-ky position (cut 4 in Fig. 4d; see Supplementary Note 9 for the band assignment), the extracted polarizations show the opposite signs. For intermediate ky values approaching the nodal plane ky ≈ 0, (also −0.5 × 2π/b) the net Sy polarization is strongly suppressed (cuts 2 and 3 in Fig. 4d), consistent with the node-like behaviour expected for an odd-parity spin texture.

Yellow and purple indicate positive and negative reduced ky, respectively, relative to each magnetic-zone centre. b, Extracted Sy polarization of spectral feature labelled α across successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The sign-changing modulation and suppression near nodal regions are consistent with the predicted p-wave spin texture. Error bars in b and shaded envelopes in d and e represent one standard deviation propagated from Poisson counting statistics. These observations are consistent with the predicted spin symmetry but do not establish an eigenstate-resolved test because the measured features contain unresolved band contributions with momentum-dependent spectral weights.

To examine the momentum dependence more systematically, we extract the energy-integrated Sy polarization of the feature labelled α within the fitting-defined integration window at photon energies from 13 eV to 23 eV, sampling successive magnetic Brillouin zones. The extracted polarization exhibits a sign-changing modulation and is strongly suppressed near the ky = 0 nodal regions (Supplementary Fig. 33 and Supplementary Note 9). Despite the finite out-of-plane momentum resolution, the observed modulation is consistent with the odd-ky spin texture expected for p-wave magnetism and with the calculated spin-polarization patterns in both the lattice and magnetic Brillouin zones (Fig. 4b,c and Supplementary Figs. 35 and 36). The variation in modulation amplitude across successive zones is also consistent with momentum-dependent unfolded spectral weights, which redistribute contributions from folded magnetic-supercell states at different extended-zone momenta (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 36). The persistence of the same sign-reversal pattern in calculations with and without SOC (Fig. 4c) further indicates that the dominant spin texture originates from magnetic symmetry rather than SOC.

According to recent reports, in addition, we find that the Sy polarization of the spectral features associated with the δ, α and γ regions remains unchanged within statistical uncertainty for symmetry-related points (kx, ky) and (−kx, ky), consistent with \(E({k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})=E(-{k}_{x},{k}_{y},{k}_{z},{S}_{y})\) (Fig. 4e).

Sources indicate that we note two limitations of the spin-ARPES analysis. First, the measured polarization is small, approximately 5%, compared with the calculated maximum contrast of about 25% (Fig. 4c), and the clearest spin-resolved features occur at finite binding energies within the near-EF electronic structure rather than at EF. The measured spin polarization may be reduced by finite energy and momentum resolution and by partial cancellation between unresolved contributions with opposite spin polarizations. Averaging over oppositely chiral magnetic domains could further reduce the signal if such domains are sampled within the illuminated area. Second, the near-EF features contain contributions from multiple folded bands with momentum-dependent spectral weights, and the cuts at positive and negative reduced ky were acquired using different photon energies and sample different extended-zone momenta, so the relative spectral weights contributing to a measured feature may differ. The measurements therefore do not constitute a one-to-one, eigenstate-resolved test of the calculated symmetry relations. In particular, the present data do not uniquely separate the momentum dependence of individual-band spin polarization from changes in the relative spectral weights of unresolved components. Within these limitations, the sign-changing Sy modulation and its suppression near the predicted nodal regions provide spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence consistent with the predicted odd-parity p-wave spin texture of the reconstructed near-EF electronic structure of EuSi.

Sources indicate that the large local magnetic moment and its strong coupling with the electronic structure enable the measurement of the magnetic domains with different chiralities using complementary probes23,24. Figure 5a shows the magnetic domains on the a–c plane measured by MFM in the conical magnetic phase, revealing a bubble-in-stripe pattern with a characteristic width of approximately 10 μm, corresponding to opposite spiral configurations. Similar stripe-like magnetic domains are observed by circularly polarized micro-ARPES with a submicrometre beam spot (Fig. 5b).

In a recent development, figure 5c,d shows the band dispersions along the \(\overline{\Gamma }-\overline{{\rm{Z}}}\) direction measured in domains A and B using right-handed and left-handed polarized light. Under circularly right-polarized illumination, FB1 and FB3 exhibit stronger spectral weight than FB2 in one domain and weaker spectral weight in the other, generating a clear domain contrast (Fig. 5c). Reversing the light polarization from circularly right-polarized to circularly left-polarized reverses this contrast, producing opposite circular-dichroism signals in domains A and B (Fig. 5e). The circular dichroism is associated with the orbital angular momentum of the Eu 4f bands with b-axis net moment25,26 (Fig. 5f and Supplementary Note 11). The calculated orbital angular momentum reverses between opposite magnetic chiralities, consistent with the observed reversal of the circular-dichroism signal. Thus, the micro-ARPES measurements reveal domains with opposite magnetic chirality and opposite b-axis moment.

In a recent development, the temperature-dependent spatial maps in Fig. 5g show that the domain contrast persists in the conical magnetic phase, weakens in the spiral magnetic phase above TN2 and disappears in the paramagnetic phase. In contrast, MFM no longer resolves the domains in the spiral magnetic phase because of the absence of a net magnetic moment detectable by this probe. The remaining circular-dichroism contrast in the spiral magnetic phase may originate from domains with different chirality, although its microscopic origin requires further scrutiny. Overall, the domain-dependent circular-dichroism demonstrates the coupling between magnetic chirality and the electronic structure. Reversing the magnetic chirality therefore reverses the circular-dichroism response of the electronic states, providing a means to probe the chirality-dependent electronic structure associated with the p-wave magnetic state.

Recent findings suggest that we now discuss the similarities and differences between p-wave magnetic spin splitting and the previously studied f-wave11 spin splitting in transition-metal dichalcogenides. Previous theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that in monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides (for example, MoS2), SOC induces odd-parity spin splitting in the valence bands27,28,29. Because this splitting is of relativistic origin in a non-magnetic crystal, it is relatively weak and cannot be easily tuned30. By contrast, first-principles calculations predict p-wave spin splitting in EuSi arising predominantly from non-relativistic exchange, whereas ARPES reveals a substantial magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure (Supplementary Table 6). Because this p-wave state originates from the chiral magnetic order, the calculated dependence of the spin texture on magnetic chirality suggests a possible route to controlling the associated spin polarization.

Industry observers note that compared with previously discussed ‘p-wave’ magnetic candidates8,9, EuSi provides a particularly clean realization of the archetypal p-wave symmetry setting8. In the spiral phase, the refined magnetic structure of stoichiometric EuSi preserves the combined \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) symmetry and has zero net magnetization, providing the symmetry setting for the predicted odd-parity p-wave spin texture without complications from finite magnetization. This combination has not been achieved in earlier candidate materials such as NiI2 or Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12. In NiI2, \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}{\boldsymbol{\tau }}\) symmetry is broken by the incommensurate non-collinear spin structure8, whereas in Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12 a weak magnetization breaks time-reversal symmetry and generates a large anomalous Hall effect9.

Furthermore, EuSi serves as an advantageous material platform because of its stoichiometric and metallic nature, and a relatively high temperature window (33.4–62 K) compared with those of low-ordering-temperature metallic counterparts such as CeNiAsO and Gd3(Ru1−δRhδ)4Al12 (approximately 8 K; see Supplementary Table 7 for detailed comparison). Taken together, these attributes position EuSi as a particularly promising material platform for exploring and ultimately harnessing p-wave magnetism in electronic structures.

Sources indicate that metallic p-wave magnets are predicted to host unconventional responses, including field-free spin-polarized transport, a large non-relativistic Edelstein effect10 and non-relativistic Ising superconductivity11. When the spiral order is canted and forms a conical state, an unconventional and large anomalous Hall effect can be observed. Analogous effects, such as the magneto-optical Kerr effect, are expected to be pronounced as well. Through combined theoretical and experimental approaches, our results provide evidence for p-wave magnetism in the electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, associated with its chiral magnetic order and combined time-reversal and lattice-translation symmetry in the spiral phase (33.4–62 K). EuSi therefore provides a realistic and accessible platform for investigating symmetry-protected transport and optical responses driven by magnetism. Beyond fundamental interest, the controllability of its metallic and chiral magnetic states may enable field-free spintronic functionalities and pave the way towards engineering p-wave-correlated and topological electronic phases in itinerant systems.

It has been revealed that euSi single crystals were grown using the Bridgman method with an Eu:Si elemental ratio of 1:1. Eu (99.95% purity) and Si (99.99% purity) were mixed and placed in a tantalum crucible. The crucible was sealed in vacuum. The sealed tube was heated to 1,450 °C for over 12 h and maintained at that temperature for 24 h. The solution was then slowly cooled to room temperature. Owing to the sensitivity of the investigated phase to oxygen and moisture, the specimen used for the single-crystal diffraction experiment was prepared (mounted) in a protective atmosphere (an argon-filled glovebox). The single crystal used for this experiment was mechanically detached (cut) from the grown single crystal and mounted in a glass capillary (0.2 mm diameter) to prevent reaction with air and moisture during the data collection. Details regarding data collection and the refinement of the crystal structure are listed in the Supplementary Tables 1–3. Low-temperature X-ray powder diffraction was carried out at beamline ID22 of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF). For this purpose, a portion of the grown single crystal was powdered, sieved through a 32-µm sieve and placed into a 0.3-mm glass capillary. The data were collected at specific temperatures using a helium-cooled cryostat and a multi-analyser stage for recording of the diffraction pattern. At temperatures below 45 K, the intensity of the beam was reduced using an attenuator to prevent the sample from heating up. The results of the low-temperature X-ray powder diffraction are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4.

According to recent reports, X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements were performed at the high-field magnet endstation of beamline I10 at Diamond Light Source, UK, with a base temperature of 5 K and magnetic field up to ±14 T along the direction of the incident beam. The crystals were cleaved in situ along the a–c (010) plane under ultrahigh vacuum, and the angle between the incident beam and the crystal (010) plane was kept at either 0° (normal incidence) or 70° (grazing incidence). X-ray absorption spectroscopy was carried out in total-electron-yield mode at the Eu M4,5 edges. X-ray magnetic circular-dichroism spectra were obtained by subtracting the absorption spectra measured with opposite helicities of the incident X-ray beam, which was aligned either parallel or antiparallel to the applied magnetic field.

Industry observers note that high-resolution ARPES measurements were performed at beamlines BL5-2 of the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL), A-branch of the Bloch beamline at MAX IV, and BL03U of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). At BL5-2, a Scienta Omicron DFS30 analyser was used, achieving an overall energy and angular resolution of 20 meV and 0.2°. At Bloch and BL03U, a Scienta Omicron DA30L analyser was used, achieving an overall energy and angular resolution of 20 meV and 0.2°. High-resolution laser-based ARPES measurements were performed on home-built set-up (hν = 6.994 eV) at ShanghaiTech University. Data were collected using an electron analyser (DA30L Scienta Omicron). The total convolved energy and angle resolution were 5 meV and 0.1°, respectively. Micro-ARPES measurements were performed at BL07U of SSRF. The beam with photon energy from 88 eV to 102 eV was focused using a Fresnel zone plate and a spatial resolution of approximately 400 nm was achieved. The data were collected by a hemispherical Scienta Omicron DA30L electron analyser. The instrument energy and momentum resolution were approximately 15 meV and 0.01 Å−1, respectively. In all set-ups, the samples were cleaved in situ at approximately 10 K and measured under ultrahigh vacuum below 5 × 10−11 torr.

The spin-resolved ARPES experiments were performed using a Scienta DA30L analyser integrated with a very-low-energy-diffraction spin detector at the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) BL13U. The samples were cleaved in situ at approximately 40 K and measured under ultrahigh vacuum below 2 × 10−10 torr. For these experiments, an effective Sherman function of 0.25 was used. Spin-resolved ARPES measurements at the U125-PGM beamline of BESSY II were performed using the spin-ARPES endstation equipped with a Scienta R4000 analyser coupled to two Mott-type spin detectors. The samples were also cleaved in situ at approximately 50 K and measured under ultrahigh vacuum below 2 × 10−10 torr. For these experiments, an effective Sherman function of 0.16 was adopted. The spin polarization was determined from \(\mathrm{Polarization}=(1/{S}_{\mathrm{eff}})\times ({I}_{\mathrm{up}}-{I}_{\mathrm{down}})/({I}_{\mathrm{up}}+{I}_{\mathrm{down}})\), in which Iup and Idown are the measured photoelectron intensities in the two spin channels and Seff is the effective Sherman function.

Sources indicate that the statistical uncertainties were estimated from the counting statistics of the two spin-detector channels. Assuming independent Poisson statistics, the measured counts Iup and Idown have standard deviations \({\sigma }_{{I}_{\mathrm{up}}}=\sqrt{{I}_{\mathrm{up}}}\) and \({\sigma }_{{I}_{\mathrm{down}}}=\sqrt{{I}_{\mathrm{down}}}\), respectively. Standard error propagation gives \({\sigma }_{{S}_{y}}=\frac{2}{{S}_{\mathrm{eff}}}\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{\mathrm{up}}{I}_{\mathrm{down}}}{{({I}_{\mathrm{up}}+{I}_{\mathrm{down}})}^{3}}}\). For energy-dependent polarization curves, this expression was applied separately to each energy bin; for the integrated polarization of a spectral feature, Iup and Idown represent the total counts accumulated within the corresponding energy-integration window. All shaded uncertainty envelopes and error bars in the spin-ARPES figures denote one standard deviation.

Neutron-diffraction experiments were conducted at the HB-3A DEMAND in the High-Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Lab. A piece of a EuSi single crystal with dimensions of approximately 4 × 3 × 0.1 mm3 was aligned in the (0KL) scattering plane and cooled. The wavelength used was 1.541 Å. The data were reduced using MANTID31 and ReTIA32. Symmetry analysis was performed using SARAh33, and magnetic-structure refinement was performed using FullProf34,35.

Sources indicate that the first-principles calculations of the band structures and Fermi surface were performed by using the first-principles DFT methods implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP)36,37. The exchange-correlation and the ion-electron interactions are treated by the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof functional38 and the projector augmented-wave method39,40 under the generalized gradient approximation. Throughout all calculations, the convergence criteria for energy are less than 2 × 10−5 eV, and the plane-wave energy cut-off is set to 400 eV. The k-point sampling uses a Monkhorst–Pack scheme41 with an accuracy of 0.02π Å−1 for self-consistent electronic calculations. To correctly describe the strong correlation effects of the Eu f orbitals, the on-site Coulomb interaction was treated using an effective Hubbard U of 5 eV.

For electrical-transport measurements, a single crystal was cut into a bar shape. A standard six-probe method was used for longitudinal resistivity and transverse Hall measurements. Electrical-transport data were collected using a physical-property measurement system (PPMS; Quantum Design). Magnetic-susceptibility and specific-heat measurements were performed using a magnetic property measurement system (MPMS; Quantum Design) and PPMS. Thermal-expansion measurements were conducted in the PPMS using a homemade capacitive dilatometer.

In a recent development, the MFM experiments were performed with a homemade helium-3 atomic force microscopy system using commercial piezoresistive cantilevers (spring constant k ≈ 3 N m−1 and resonant frequency approximately 43 kHz). The tips were coated with a nominally 100-nm-thick cobalt layer by magnetron sputtering. The MFM data were acquired by Nanonis SPM Controllers (SPECS) with a phase-locked loop. The MFM signal, the resonant frequency shift of the cantilever, is proportional to the out-of-plane stray field gradient generated by the sample. By using the constant-height mode, MFM images are acquired on a scanning plane approximately 200 nm above the surface.
